fixes.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, never comes up in these verses. Paul says that before their very eyes, "Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified." I get the guess, since the law is all over this passage. But the picture Paul holds up is the cross, not the mountain.

Abraham does show up later in this passage, but not for that. His offering of Isaac, his son, is told in Genesis 22, and Paul doesn't bring it up here. What Paul says was portrayed before the Galatians' eyes is Jesus Christ as crucified. Keep that one on the counter, baker.

Paul asks if they received the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith. He's steering them toward hearing with faith. I think he's pointing at an answer that's sitting in plain sight. It's like asking a friend who ate the last cookie while crumbs sit on their shirt.

Paul asks whether they, after starting in the Spirit, are now finishing in the flesh. That question points to a change of direction from how they began. It's like starting a batch with the oven preheated and then finishing it on the countertop. Paul's question is all about that turn.

Paul never talks about speed here. His words are about where they started and where they're finishing: "After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?" The question he asks is about direction, not pace, baker.
Paul says God lavishes His Spirit on them and works miracles among them. Then he asks if that's because they practice the law, or because they hear and believe. The word lavish is a big one, friend.

Visions don't show up in Paul's question, friend. He says God lavishes His Spirit on them and works miracles among them. Then he asks whether that's because they practice the law, or because they hear and believe. Visions were a fun guess, but the word in the verse is miracles.

Fear isn't the word here, baker, though it's a fair guess from a stamper who gets nervous around a hot oven. Paul quotes, "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." The word doing the work is believed. That's what the credit came with.

"All nations will be blessed through you." Paul says the Scripture foretold the gospel to Abraham in those words. He calls it the gospel, and he says it was told ahead of time. That's a very wide promise, friend.

Paul quotes, "Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law." That's all of it, not just a part. He says all who rely on works of the law are under a curse. So the word in the verse is everything, baker.

Works isn't the word in the line Paul quotes. He says no one is justified before God by the law, because "The righteous will live by faith." So the word is faith. That's the verse he gives to back it up.
Paul says the opposite. He writes, "The law, however, is not based on faith…" Then he quotes, "The man who does these things will live by them." The law is about doing. So this one is false, friend.
Right, Paul says, "The law, however, is not based on faith…" He follows it by quoting, "The man who does these things will live by them." The law is about doing. Faith is a different road.

Abraham is in this passage, but not as the one who redeems. Paul says the blessing was promised to him (Galatians 3:14) and calls him the man of faith (Galatians 3:9). The one who redeemed us from the curse of the law is Christ. That's verse 13.

Paul says Christ redeemed us "…in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus…" That's the reason he gives. The blessing promised to Abraham reaches the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so this one is true, friend.
